Learning Objectives
Identify the epidemiology, pathoanatomy, and risk factors for anterior shoulder instability.
Discuss the mechanism and direction of shoulder instability.
Perform relevant physical examination maneuvers.
Recognize injury patterns and bone loss on imaging studies and apply appropriate treatment
options based on patient factors and imaging findings.
Review appropriate nonsurgical and surgical management of anterior shoulder instability.
Epidemiology and Overview
Incidence—Traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation is the most common form of
glenohumeral instability, representing 88% to 98% of all dislocations.

Age at the time of the initial dislocation has been considered the primary risk factor for re-

Risk factors for recurrence include:
Age at initial injury
Sex
Activity level (ie, contact versus noncontact athletics)
Presence of bony lesions of the humeral head and glenoid
High recurrence rates (>80%) are observed in younger patients, males, and contact athletes,
especially with the presence of a glenoid or humeral head bony defect.
Lower recurrence rates (<10%) are observed in older patients, females, and those with an
absence of glenoid or humeral head bony defects.

Epidemiology and Overview
The glenohumeral joint is the most dislocated joint in the human body because of the
relative lack of bony constraint, and an extensive range of motion (ROM) imparted by the
shallow ball and socket joint2,3 (Resource 1). The most common form of shoulder
instability, including dislocation and subluxation, is in the anterior direction after
traumatic injury.4,5 The estimated incidence of acute shoulder dislocations requiring
medical intervention is 23.9 per 100,000 person-years, with males accounting for 70% to
85% of all injuries.5-7 Almost one-half of all acute traumatic anterior shoulder
dislocations occur in patients aged 15 to 29 years and result from injury during sports
activity or recreation.6 The incidence rate for anterior shoulder dislocations among
collegiate athletes is 0.12 per 1,000 athlete exposures, with an incidence rate ratio of
2.67 for male versus female athletes and a predominance of injuries occurring during
contact sports, including football, wrestling, and ice hockey.7
The passive anterior restraints to the glenohumeral joint often are disrupted after
primary shoulder dislocation. According to a systematic review, a 39% rate of recurrent
instability is reported after an acute first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation.1
Increased rates of recurrent instability were associated with age 40 years or younger,
male sex, and individuals with soft-tissue hyperlaxity.1 Conversely, lower recurrence
rates are observed in older patients, females, and those who have injuries without

associated glenoid or humeral head bone loss. Hovelius et al8 reported increased
recurrent instability rates in patients younger than 25 years who were treated
nonsurgically and decreased recurrence rates in patients who had an associated greater
tuberosity fracture at time of dislocation. Anatomic factors, such as increased glenoid
anteversion, inferior inclination, the glenoid height-to-width ratio, and the humeral
containing angle, have been associated with an increased risk of anteroinferior
glenohumeral dislocation.9-13
Pathoanatomy
Anterior glenohumeral dislocation typically occurs secondary to a traumatic event that leads to
excessive abduction and external rotation, thereby resulting in anterior and inferior
displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid.
A Bankart lesion (detachment of the anteroinferior labrum and the anterior band of the
inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL) complex) (Figure 1) iis an important pathoanatomic
finding that is present in 90% of all patients with a traumatic glenohumeral dislocation.

capsulolabral complex. G = glenoid, L = labrum. (Reproduced from Andelman SM, Mazzocca

Pathoanatomy
Most anterior glenohumeral instability events are subluxations, in which a portion of the
glenohumeral joint articular surface maintains contact during anterior translation of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:35 AM
AAOS | Shoulder: Anterior Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000570
7/37

humerus.3 The capsulolabral soft-tissue and osseous restraints of the shoulder joint
often are damaged during traumatic dislocation or subluxation of the glenohumeral
joint, which places the patient at risk for additional instability. The most common intra-
articular injury associated with anterior instability is avulsion of the anteroinferior
glenoid labrum and the anterior band of the IGHL complex, referred to as a Bankart
lesion.14 A Bankart lesion may involve a soft-tissue or bony avulsion. Owens et al15
reported that 96% of athletes who experienced a first-time subluxation event had
evidence of a Bankart lesion on imaging studies and/or surgical treatment. Disruption
and stretching of anterior capsulolabral soft tissue and loss of more than 20% of the
width of the anterior glenoid alter the biomechanics of the glenohumeral joint and are
risk factors for recurrent anterior instability.1,16
The anteroinferior labrum is the soft-tissue structure most commonly injured during
traumatic anterior subluxation or dislocation; however, other capsular structures may
fail during acute trauma. In an anterior labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsion, the
torn labrum displaces along the medial aspect of the glenoid neck and heals under a
portion of avulsed but intact periosteum, which may make surgical repair of the anterior
labrum more challenging.2 Damage to other static stabilizers of the glenohumeral joint,
primarily the glenohumeral ligaments, also may place patients at risk for recurrent
instability. The anterior band of the IGHL is the primary capsular ligamentous restraint to
anterior humeral subluxation.17 The IGHL fails most often during traumatic anterior
dislocation in a process known as HAGL; however, it also may fail, more rarely, via
glenoid avulsion of the glenohumeral ligaments.17,18 HAGL lesions may include failure of
the anterior ligament band or, less commonly, the posterior ligament band, either of
which may extend into the capsulolabral complex.17 Identification of injuries to the
capsulolabral complex and knowledge of normal anatomic variants, such as a cordlike
middle glenohumeral complex (Buford complex),19 is critical to restore the soft-tissue
restraints to anterior shoulder instability.
Injury to the rotator cuff during traumatic anterior subluxation or dislocation in the
young athletic population is rare; however, surgeons should maintain a high suspicion
for a rotator cuff tear in patients older than 40 years who sustain a traumatic first-time
anterior shoulder dislocation.20-22 Older patients are more likely to sustain a traumatic
disruption of the rotator cuff or a fracture of the greater tuberosity without concomitant
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:35 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000570
8/37

injury to the anterior labrum.21 In a large prospective database study, Robinson et al23
identified a rotator cuff tear or greater tuberosity fracture via ultrasonography in 33.4%
of all patients (mean age = 47.6 years) who underwent reduction for an acute anterior
shoulder dislocation. Timely identification and subsequent surgical repair of the acutely
torn rotator cuff after dislocation will help restore dynamic stabilization of the shoulder
joint.
Brachial plexus injuries have been identified in as many as 13.5% of patients after
reduction of a traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation.23 Most nerve injuries occur in the
infrascapular region of the brachial plexus and most commonly involve the axillary
nerve.24 Risk factors for nerve injury include older patient age, higher-energy trauma,
and greater time to reduction. Traction injuries to the brachial plexus often resolve
without management; however, 13% to 18% of patients require surgical treatment if no
signs of recovery are observed, typically 3 to 6 months after nerve injury.24
A risk of injury to the bone at the humeral head and the glenoid exists. An anterior
dislocation of the glenohumeral joint will put the posterior humeral head in contact with
the anterior glenoid rim, which may result in an impaction defect or a compression
fracture at the posterior humeral head that is called a Hill-Sachs lesion. Hill-Sachs lesions
have been reported in as many as 90% of first-time dislocation events.15 Recurrent
anterior shoulder instability may continue to cause loss of humeral head bone beyond
that lost during the initial dislocation event if the humeral head lesion engages with
anterior glenoid.25 Risk of engagement of a Hill-Sachs lesion is defined by a glenoid
track, characterized by the zone of contact between the humeral head and the glenoid
with the arm in the abducted and externally rotated position.25-27 As the posterior
humeral head contacts the anterior glenoid rim during dislocation, it may cause an acute
fracture of the glenoid, known as a bony Bankart or a Bankart fracture. Progressive
attritional anteroinferior glenoid bone loss may occur with recurrent instability or
because of repetitive engagement of the humeral head within the glenoid track.28

Evaluation
Evaluation of patients with anterior shoulder instability should include a thorough
history and clinical examination of both shoulders to guide appropriate diagnosis and
management. History regarding a specific instability event should include the acuity,
which ranges from acute dislocation to recurrent atraumatic subluxation; the
mechanism of instability (eg, a young collision athlete versus an elderly patient who fell
from a standing position); and the direction of instability.29 In patients with prior
instability, surgeons must elucidate the natural history of shoulder instability, including
the age at and circumstance of the first instability event, the number and frequency of
prior instances of instability, the mechanism and causative position of instability, and
prior treatment options (including nonsurgical reductions and surgical management).30
Surgeons also must understand a patient’s hand dominance, levels of activity and
sporting competition, occupation, and medical history, and must inquire specifically
about soft-tissue laxity and hypermobility.
Physical examination should begin with a general assessment and observation of the
patient. A patient with an acutely anteriorly dislocated shoulder will most likely be seen
in the emergency department, and the patient will have a clear deformity about the
shoulder with prominence anteriorly. The arm will be in the adducted and externally

9/4/26, 9:35 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000570
11/37

rotated position. A careful neurovascular examination is important before and after
reduction. For patients seeking care in clinic for symptoms of anterior shoulder
instability, the clinician should begin with inspection of the shoulder for deformity or
scapular dyskinesia. Generalized hyperlaxity should be assessed via Beighton criteria
because patients with hyperlaxity are as much as 2.7 times more likely to have
glenohumeral instability.1,31 Active and passive ROM and rotator cuff strength of the
injured shoulder should be assessed and compared to that of the contralateral shoulder.
Special tests for anterior shoulder instability include the sulcus, Gagey, load-and-shift,
apprehension, and relocation tests.
The Gagey hyperabduction test is used to assess inferior instability and disruption of the IGHL.
For the load-and-shift test, lateral pressure is first applied to the humeral head to center it in
the glenoid; then the humeral head is translated anteriorly and posteriorly to determine the
degree of translation from minimal to fully dislocated.32
The apprehension test is performed with the patient in the supine position; the shoulder is
brought to 90° of abduction and 90° of external rotation, thereby placing an anterior moment
or force on the proximal humerus. The test result is positive if the patient feels apprehensive
and experiences symptoms of anterior instability.
The apprehension test is followed by the relocation test, in which a posteriorly directed force is
applied at the proximal humerus with a maintained arm position of 90° of abduction and 90°
of external rotation, with symptoms of apprehension being relieved.2,32

Radiography
Imaging for anterior shoulder instability should begin with plain radiographs, including
AP, Grashey, scapular Y, and axillary lateral views. This series will allow for initial
evaluation of the glenohumeral joint alignment and assessment for associated fractures,
including bony avulsions. An AP view can be obtained to visualize humeral head
impaction fractures and glenoid rim fractures (Video 1). For patients who cannot be
adequately positioned for an axillary lateral view because of pain or risk of instability, a
modified lateral Velpeau view may allow for assessment of axial joint alignment with the
patient’s arm remaining in a sling.33 The West Point axillary view is a tangential view of
the anteroinferior glenoid rim obtained with the arm abducted 70° to 90° and is useful in
evaluating bone loss in patients with a bony Bankart lesion.34,35 The Stryker notch view
is obtained by placing the cassette under the affected shoulder with the palm of the
hand placed on the forehead and the X-ray beam tilted 10° toward the head, centered
over the coracoid process.34 This view helps to visualize the posterolateral aspect of the
humeral head to detect Hill-Sachs defects or flattening of the posterolateral humeral
head.35

Computed Tomography
Advanced imaging studies ae useful for evaluating osseous and soft-tissue injuries. CT is
essential to quantifying glenoid bone loss in patients with an acute bony Bankart
fracture or chronic erosion of the anteroinferior glenoid because of recurrent instability.
Glenoid bone loss may be calculated on three-dimensional CT via various methods, and

the calculated percentage of bone loss will help guide management. Various methods
have been proposed to calculate glenoid bone loss based on CT cross-sections;1,36
however, the more recent development and use of three-dimensional CT reconstructed
images with subtraction of the humerus allow for digital measurement of the percentage
bone loss from the articulating portion of the glenoid, defined as a circle fit to the
inferior two-thirds of the glenoid.35,37 Loss of more than 20% to 25% of the glenoid
surface area is a major risk factor for recurrent instability.36 Although 20% to 25%
represents a critical value for which bone loss should be addressed in a primary surgical
procedure, a subcritical threshold of 13.5% bone loss has been shown to lead to
unacceptable clinical outcome scores, regardless of recurrent instability.38 CT also may
be useful in determining the size and extent of bone loss to the humeral head in a Hill-
Sachs lesion and whether a Hill-Sachs lesion engages with the Bankart lesion (Video 2).28
If a posterior Hill-Sachs lesion engages with the anterior glenoid lesion during functional
abduction and external rotation about the shoulder, it is referred to an off-track lesion; a
Hill-Sachs lesion is an on-track lesion if it does not engage during shoulder ROM28 (Video
3).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Useful for soft-tissue detail, labral lesions, HAGL lesions, and capsular tears
Intra-articular contrast increases the sensitivity of detecting soft-tissue injuries.
Helpful in assessing concomitant rotator cuff tears

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI commonly is performed to aid in the diagnosis and management of anterior
shoulder instability because it can be used to evaluate the integrity of the soft-tissue
structures, including the capsulolabral complex, rotator cuff, and articular cartilage. MRI
is useful in younger patients to diagnose lesions of the anterior capsule and labrum,
primarily Bankart lesions (Video 1). The addition of intra-articular contrast in magnetic
resonance arthrography will enhance visualization of specific lesions, including Bankart

lesions, superior labrum anterior to posterior lesions, HAGL lesions, and anterior
labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsions.35 A HAGL lesion can be visualized on a
magnetic resonance arthrogram; the typical U-shaped pouch at the inferior glenoid and
the adjacent margin of the humeral head is converted to a J-shape, with concurrent
contrast extravasation anteriorly or posteriorly on an axial view representing disruption
of the anterior or posterior IGHL band, respectively.17 In older patients who sustain an
acute anterior shoulder dislocation and experience subsequent shoulder pain and
weakness, MRI is critical to facilitate evaluation for an acute associated rotator cuff tear.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is a reasonable treatment option for patients with a first-time
anterior dislocation; however, patients should be counseled on the high rates of re-dislocation
based on demographic criteria. A brief 1- to 3-week period of immobilization is followed by
ROM exercises.

Nonsurgical Management
A neurovascular examination should be performed and documented before reduction.
Closed reduction should be attempted after an anterior dislocation is confirmed via a
physical examination and/or imaging studies and lack of crepitus is confirmed via
physical examination or a fracture is confirmed via radiographs.39 Immediate or early
reduction, such that performed on the sideline in patients with a sports injury, often
facilitates easier reduction before muscle spasm. Various reduction maneuvers and
modifications have been described,40,41 and the treating clinician should use the
technique with which they are best trained and most comfortable. A complete
description of each reduction technique with technical photos can be found in a
comprehensive review article by Gottlieb et al.41 Traditional reduction maneuvers
associated with high levels of success include the traction-countertraction technique; the
fast, reliable, and safe technique; the Milch technique; and the Stimson technique. For
the traction-countertraction technique, a folded sheet is placed around the patient’s
torso on the affected side and the extremity is abducted to 90°. One clinician pulls
longitudinal traction on the affected extremity while another clinician holds
countertraction on the sheet on the contralateral side. Gentle internal rotation, external
rotation, or manual anterior pressure may be used to assist reduction41 (Figure 10;
Video 4). For the fast, reliable, and safe technique, the patient lays in the supine position
and the clinician grasps the affected wrist with both hands, keeping the elbow extended
and the forearm in neutral rotation. The extremity is gradually abducted via gentle
longitudinal traction while the examiner oscillates the extremity 5 cm in the
cranial/caudal plane at a frequency of 2 to 3 cm per second. When the extremity is in 90°
of abduction, the clinician externally rotates the extremity while continuing traction,
abduction, and oscillation. Reduction should occur at 120° abduction, at which time the
clinician internally rotates the shoulder, flexes the elbow, and brings the extremity over
the chest.41, 42 For the Milch technique, the patient is placed in the supine position with
the head of the bed flat or elevated 30°. The clinician places one hand in the affected
axilla with palpation of the medial border of the humeral anteriorly. The clinician grasps
the wrist with their other hand and gradually brings the extremity into abduction while
applying medial and cranial pressure to the humeral head. Once in full overhead
abduction, the extremity is externally rotated and gentle in-line traction is applied, which

Management for anterior shoulder instability is dictated by differentiating a first-time
dislocation or subluxation event from recurrent chronic anterior instability. A trial of
nonsurgical treatment is indicated in most patients with a first-time anterior dislocation;
however, early surgical treatment is indicated in patients who are at high risk for
recurrent instability—those who are younger, male, and/or contact athletes—especially
in the presence of bone loss.1,2,8 Athletes who sustain a first-time dislocation during a
sporting season may opt for delayed surgical treatment with brief immobilization and
early rehabilitation because of specific circumstances, such as recruiting or a final
season; however, early surgical management generally is recommended to prevent
additional damage to the glenohumeral joint.29 Patients with a first-time dislocation in
whom a trial of nonsurgical treatment is indicated include those older than 35 to 40
years, sedentary younger adults, noncontact athletes, and patients with hypermobility
and multidirectional instability.1,30 Nonsurgical management typically consists of
immobilization for 1 to 3 weeks, dependent on patient factors, followed by early ROM,
with or without physical therapy. Immobilization in external rotation has been shown to
maintain a displaced anteroinferior labrum in closer opposition to the glenoid rim;
however, a meta-analysis of six randomized clinical studies43 did not find clinical benefit

glenohumeral joint.
Surgical Management
Indications for surgical treatment are as follows:
Failed nonsurgical management with recurrent instability
Patients younger than 25 years who engage in athletic activities (especially contact sports) or
other high-demand activities; such patients may benefit from immediate surgical stabilization
Substantial bony injuries or rotator cuff tears require immediate surgical stabilization

Surgical Management
Early surgical treatment is indicated for young athletes, high-demand patients, patients
with substantial anterior glenoid bone loss, and patients with a concomitant rotator cuff
tear.1,2,8 Surgical treatment also is indicated in patients with recurrent instability, which
commonly results from bone loss and damage to the static stabilizers of the
glenohumeral joint. With repeated episodes of anterior subluxation or dislocation, the
glenohumeral joint is at risk of progressive bone loss to the anterior glenoid and the
humeral head, and the degree of bone loss is one of the most important factors in
surgical planning and success.36

The goal of surgical management for anterior shoulder instability is to provide static
stabilization via repair or reconstruction of damaged structures of the anterior inferior
glenohumeral joint and the posterior humeral head, if indicated. A universal surgical
approach does not exist to manage anterior instability because the indicated surgical
procedure will differ based on the degree of bony deficiency, the presence of bipolar
glenoid and humeral lesions, surgeon experience with reconstruction techniques, and
patient factors.36

Bankart Repair
The preferred treatment option for anterior capsulolabral injuries—including Bankart
lesions, bony Bankart lesions involving less than 15% of the glenoid surface, concurrent
superior labrum anterior to posterior tears, and posterior HAGL lesions—is arthroscopic
repair, with or without capsulorrhaphy. Patients with an anterior HAGL lesion may be
more likely to require open surgical treatment, particularly if a concurrent subscapularis
tear is present or anterior glenoid bone grafting is necessary.38 Equivalent recurrence
rates have been reported between arthroscopic and open Bankart repair, and
arthroscopy is associated with a 1.8-fold decrease in surgical time and a 10-fold decrease
in surgical blood loss.45 Arthroscopic surgical Bankart repair includes release,
mobilization, and débridement of the anterior labrum, followed by repair and tensioning
of the anteroinferior capsulolabral complex46 (Resources 2 and 3). If performed in
appropriately indicated patients, arthroscopic Bankart repair is associated with a high
success rate, with an overall anterior instability recurrence rate of 4% to 19%.46 A
reported 97.5% rate of return to sports activity has been reported after arthroscopic
Bankart repair.45,47
Open Bone Transfer

Open Bone Transfer
Management of glenoid bone deficiency depends on the percentage of bone loss at the
anterior glenoid, whether a discrete bony fragment is present after an acute instability
event, and patient-specific factors. The percentage of bone loss because of recurrent
instability may be characterized as minimal (<15%), moderate (15% to 30%), or severe
(>30%), and management differs based on glenoid deficiency, with moderate lesions
managed via open coracoid transfer, known as a Latarjet procedure, and severe lesions
managed via open bone grafting36,37 (Resources 4 through 6).

Hill-Sachs Lesions

Hill-Sachs Lesions
Surgical management of Hill-Sachs lesions via tissue-filling methods (including
remplissage), humeral head bone grafting, or humeral head resurfacing is indicated for
the management of engaging off-track lesions with concurrent management of mild to
moderate glenoid defects.25 Remplissage, performed open or arthroscopically according
to the method for Bankart repair, is the most commonly performed procedure and
includes capsulotenodesis of the posterior capsule and the infraspinatus tendon to fill
the lesion of posterior humeral head and prevent engagement with the anterior
glenoid29 (Resource 7). Open repair of a larger glenoid lesion via bone augmentation will
provide enough bone stock to prevent engagement of the Hill-Sachs lesion, converting
the humeral defect to an on-track lesion, which does not require independent
management. If a displaced glenoid fragment is present after an acute traumatic
dislocation, open reduction and internal fixation of the fragment will restore stability.
More commonly, bone is missing because of attritional wear; therefore, autograft or
allograft bone is necessary for augmentation. Latarjet, open coracoid transfer, is the
most used and well-studied bone graft, demonstrating efficacious and long-term
restoration of joint stability. Alternative options for bone augmentation from grafts that
closely match the contour of the anterior glenoid include autograft from the inner table
of the iliac crest, distal tibia allograft, and glenoid allograft36,37 (Resources 3 through 5).
Complications
Recurrence of instability—Large-scale studies suggest near-equivalent rates of recurrence
between arthroscopic (4% to 15%) and open (5% to 10%) repair.
Stiffness because of overtightening of the capsulolabral complex
Subscapularis failure with open surgical techniques
Axillary nerve injury: rare but possible complication because of nerve proximity to the inferior
joint capsule
Infection

Complications
The main complication after surgical management for anterior instability is recurrence of
instability, including dislocation or subluxation. Reported recurrence rates range from
4% to 19%.46 Boileau et al48 reported a 15% recurrence rate after arthroscopic Bankart
repair and found that risk of recurrence was associated with glenoid or humeral bone
loss that was not adequately addressed and associated with patients treated with the
use of three or fewer suture anchors. Additional risk factors for recurrent instability after
arthroscopic repair include age younger than 22 years at time of first dislocation, male
sex, and time from initial injury to surgical management of more than 6 months.11
Longer term follow-up has demonstrated that as many as 26% of patients experience
early osteoarthritis of the glenohumeral joint after undergoing treatment for anterior
instability, with risk factors including number of preoperative dislocations, age, and
number of anchors used for repair.46,49 Although adequate lesion repair and fixation is
necessary to prevent recurrence, overtightening of the anteroinferior capsule may lead
to postoperative stiffness. Open procedures, most commonly performed for glenoid
augmentation, also are associated with a risk of recurrent instability, for which
hyperlaxity, bilateral instability, and female sex are risk factors.50 In addition, open
procedures are associated with a risk for subscapularis failure, leading to recurrent
anterior instability to the point that a lesser tuberosity osteotomy, a subscapularis peel,
or a subscapularis tenotomy with subsequent repair is necessary to access the joint.
Finally, a rare but possible complication of arthroscopic or open surgical management
for anterior instability is axillary nerve injury, which has been reported at a rate of 0.2%
to 0.3%.46,51 The axillary nerve courses from anterior to posterior within 1 to 4 mm of
the inferior capsule.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Failure to reconstruct and re-tension the anteroinferior capsulolabral complex
Failure to recognize and manage glenoid or humeral bony defects

Pearls and Pitfalls
Successful surgical management depends on treatment decisions made during the
preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative periods. Success in the preoperative
period includes the correct diagnosis of anterior instability based on the patient history,
physical examination, and thorough evaluation of preoperative imaging studies to
determine the indicated surgical procedure. The primary reason for recurrence of
anterior instability is failure to sufficiently manage glenoid and/or humeral bone loss,
and appropriate indications are of utmost importance in considering surgical
management. Pearls and pitfalls for successful outcomes based on the intraoperative
period include details regarding technical proficiency. Careful consideration of portal and
anchor placement and use of a sufficient number of anchors will aid in successful
arthroscopic Bankart repair (Video 7). Appropriate progression toward ROM,
strengthening, and return to sports activity are aided by standardization of rehabilitation
protocols in the postoperative period and the physical therapist’s familiarity with the
surgical anatomy and procedure.52
